Non-aluminium proxy values and engineering estimates are explicitly labeled to prevent unsupported transfer.*

---

### 1. Melt Pool Geometry and Thermal Characteristics

**Width, depth, and length.** For AlSi10Mg on 30 µm layers with a 108 µm beam spot, experimentally measured single-track melt pool dimensions at scan speeds of ~0.55–0.92 m/s and powers of 200–350 W give depths of approximately 65–90 µm and widths of approximately 185–240 µm (pqac-00000001). At the lower scan speed (0.55 m/s, 100 µs exposure), depths reach ~80–88 µm and widths ~220–231 µm. Melt pool length is not independently reported in the retrieved AlSi10Mg literature at these conditions; it is typically 2–4× the width based on cross-material LPBF experience but must be verified for Al alloys at this operating point.

**Conduction-to-keyhole thresholds.** A melt pool depth-to-width aspect ratio of ~0.4 has been proposed as a practical conduction-to-transition/keyhole threshold for aluminium alloys, with rounded keyhole-associated defects appearing at or above this ratio (pqac-00000000). The widely cited normalised enthalpy threshold of ΔH/h_s ≈ 10 marks the onset of keyholing (pqac-00000000). The keyhole number Ke, as defined by Gan et al. and reproduced by Huang et al., is Ke ≈ (1/√π)(ΔH/h_m), and the tangent of the front keyhole wall angle scales approximately linearly with Ke across multiple alloys and processing conditions (pqac-00000018). For bare Al 1100 at 1.5 m/s, the experimentally observed keyhole onset occurs at 265 ± 15 W (with the keyhole transition spanning roughly 250–400 W), while melting onset is at ~100 W (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000039).

**Absorptivity at ~1070 nm.** The calculated flat-surface absorptivity of aluminium at ~1.07 µm is only 0.047, while multiple-scattering in the powder bed raises total absorptivity to ~0.22 — approximately 4.7× the flat value (pqac-00000036). In-situ calorimetry by Trapp et al. found that a ~100 µm powder layer has approximately twice the absorptivity of a polished bare disc at low power. Once the powder track fully melts, absorptivity drops sharply, then rises again as keyhole formation develops, eventually saturating at ~0.78 in the deep-keyhole regime (pqac-00000038). Patel & Vlasea adopt effective values of ~0.15 (conduction), ~0.425 (transition), and ~0.70 (keyhole) for aluminium alloys (pqac-00000034). These values are substantially lower than those for steels and Ti-6Al-4V in conduction mode (steel flat absorptivity ~0.3 versus Al ~0.05), but converge in keyhole mode (~0.7–0.8 for all materials).

**Peak surface temperature.** The plume temperature near the melt-pool surface has been modelled at ~3360 K for a laser-metal interaction in argon, approximately uniform over the first few millimetres of plume height (pqac-00000014). For aluminium, the boiling point is ~2743 K; keyhole-mode surface temperatures therefore reach well above this.

**Marangoni surface-flow velocities.** No direct AlSi10Mg melt-pool surface velocity measurement was retrieved. Melt flow velocities up to ~5 m/s have been cited in the context of Al-alloy spatter studies (pqac-00000015). CFD simulations for Al alloys typically report Marangoni-driven velocities of 0.5–3 m/s; this remains a data gap for direct experimental validation at LPBF-relevant Al conditions.

**Cooling rates, G and R.** Cooling rates for AlSi10Mg LPBF have been estimated at 8.3 ± 2.0 × 10⁵ K/s (melt pool centre) and 1.6–4.4 × 10⁵ K/s (melt pool boundary) from cell-size-based semi-empirical and numerical models (pqac-00000040). Thermal simulations over a range of energy inputs (700–1900 J/m) give 1.35–3.91 × 10⁵ K/s, with cooling rate decreasing as energy input increases (pqac-00000042). Analytical models extending to 250–450 W and 0.2–1.5 m/s calculate cooling rates up to ~1.2–1.75 × 10⁶ K/s (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000044). No independently measured numerical G (K/m) and R (m/s) pair for AlSi10Mg was retrieved; the relationship Ṫ = G·R holds, with R locally bounded by the scan velocity (pqac-00000041, pqac-00000045). These cooling rates are broadly similar to those for steels and Ti-6Al-4V at comparable energy densities, though aluminium's higher thermal conductivity shifts the absolute values.

**Keyhole oscillation frequencies and porosity windows.** Huang et al. report keyhole radial fluctuations spanning 2.5–10 kHz, with the highest frequencies (~10 kHz) occurring in the transition regime (regime II) between stable and unstable keyholing, using 200–500 W and 0.6–1.6 m/s (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020). For aluminium LPBF specifically, Guo et al. identify a pore-free region below ~0.020 MJ/cm³ linear energy density, with rapid keyhole oscillation onset near ~0.026 MJ/cm³ (pqac-00000006). Keyhole-penetration pores (KP-pores) form when oscillations cause the keyhole to exceed the melt-pool depth, while RF-pores and R-pores form via liquid-bridge pinch-off and rear-wall humps respectively (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000007).

---

### 2. Vapour Plume

**Plume height, velocity, and tilt.** High-speed CCD imaging of LPBF plumes reports dimensions of approximately 4–5 mm in length and ~1.5 mm in width (pqac-00000013). Measured steady ascent velocities range from 38 m/s at 0.57 MW/cm² to 97 m/s at 1.14 MW/cm² (pqac-00000014). The vapour-jet velocity at the melt-pool surface is of order 20–300 m/s (pqac-00000015). With an argon cross-flow of ~2.1 m/s, the plume propagates upward only ~1 mm before its momentum is comparable to the cross-flow; without cross-flow, it rises higher and trails fume (pqac-00000029). Schlieren imaging shows the plume tilts backward at higher scan speeds (pqac-00000028). A practical cross-flow of 2–5 m/s is recommended: too little allows fume accumulation and laser obstruction; too much disturbs the powder bed (pqac-00000030).

**Plume temperature.** Modelled at ~3360 K near the melt-pool surface (pqac-00000014).

**Composition (Mg and Zn enrichment and loss).** For AlSi10Mg, Mg losses of ~57% of the initial Mg content have been reported during IR-laser LPBF. For AA6061, ~17% Mg loss; for AA7075, ~19% Mg loss and ~3% Zn loss in one study, though Zn losses up to ~30% are cited elsewhere due to Zn's lower boiling point (~907 °C vs ~1090 °C for Mg) (pqac-00000021). Green-laser processing at lower energy density reduces these losses. The vapour is therefore strongly enriched in Mg relative to the bulk alloy, and in Zn for 7xxx alloys.

**Plasma formation at ~1 µm wavelength.** No direct evidence of a laser-sustained plasma (inverse bremsstrahlung absorption) at 1 µm CW LPBF conditions was retrieved for aluminium alloys. The plume is widely described as a weakly ionised metal vapour rather than a true plasma at these power densities. CW fibre-laser LPBF at 200–500 W does not reach the threshold for significant inverse bremsstrahlung at 1.07 µm in argon; this contrasts with pulsed Nd:YAG or CO₂ laser welding where plasma formation is more readily observed.

**Spectral emission lines.** For Al7075 DED (not LPBF), Ren et al. report emission lines of Al I (396.054 nm), Mg I (383.229 nm), and Cr I in the visible range. These principal Al and Mg lines fall below 600 nm and would therefore be outside the user's proposed 600–1000 nm and 1.3–1.7 µm detector bands. No validated Al-LPBF spectral line list for the 600–1000 nm or 1.3–1.7 µm ranges was retrieved — this is an explicit data gap. Weak Na I (589 nm) and K I (766–770 nm) lines from trace impurities in the powder could potentially fall in the 600–1000 nm band but have not been documented for LPBF Al alloys.

**Beam attenuation by the plume.** No quantitative percentage of beam attenuation by the plume was retrieved for Al LPBF. Qualitatively, accumulated fume from prior tracks can "seriously block" the laser when cross-flow is insufficient, while adequate cross-flow (~2–5 m/s) convects products away and maintains repeatable conditions (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030). For steels and Ti-6Al-4V, plume attenuation of a few percent per pass is commonly cited in the welding literature; Al alloys may produce less dense metal vapour per unit energy due to lower absorptivity in conduction mode, but this remains unquantified.

---

### 3. Condensate (Soot)

**Primary particle and agglomerate sizes.** For LPBF of stainless steel (the best-characterised system), TEM analysis shows primary condensate nanoparticles with equivalent projected-area diameters predominantly 4–16 nm, with a median of ~9.4 nm (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000025). These form fractal-like chain agglomerates ranging from ~0.5 µm to >10 µm in length (pqac-00000024). Rare coarser particles of 0.7–2 µm were also observed on filters (pqac-00000025). Particles >30 nm retain a metallic core with an oxide shell (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027). **No equivalent Al-alloy condensate characterisation was retrieved** — this is a significant data gap. Al condensate is expected to form alumina-rich nanoparticles due to Al's high oxygen affinity; primary particle sizes may be comparable or slightly larger than steel fume particles.

**Mass generation rate.** No quantitative mass generation rate per unit track length or per joule was retrieved for any Al alloy. This is a critical missing measurement for window-contamination modelling.

**Window/cover-slide transmission loss.** No published measurement of cover-slide transmission loss per build hour for Al LPBF was found. This quantity is geometry- and flow-dependent and must be measured for the specific chamber configuration.

---

### 4. Spatter

**Ejection velocities and angles for Al alloys.** For Al-Fe-Zr LPBF (synchrotron X-ray imaging), at 350–500 W and 800 mm/s, the mean spatter trajectory angle is approximately −10° to −25° (backward), with 70–80% of ejecta being backward spatter; at 500 mm/s the mean angle approaches 0° (more vertical) (pqac-00000015). An example laser–spatter interaction accelerated a ~36 µm particle from 0.57 to 3.39 m/s over 350 µs (pqac-00000016). Vapour-jet velocities of 20–300 m/s drive the ejection. For AlSi10/AlSi7, mean spatter velocity increases linearly with laser intensity, and over half of detected spatters have radii <30 µm at 4.24 MW/cm²; particles with radii >70–80 µm occur in all tested conditions (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). AlSi7 produces ~30% more spatters than AlSi10 at 5.66 MW/cm² (pqac-00000010).

**Solid vs liquid spatter.** In Al-Fe-Zr, solid spatter constitutes >82% of all ejecta; jet spatter is ~2% (pqac-00000017). The wide, shallow vapour depression zone in conduction-mode Al melting promotes backward liquid droplets that can exceed 90% of the liquid fraction (pqac-00000015).

**Comparison with steels and Ti-6Al-4V.** Approximately 90% of melt-pool ejections in LPBF generally fall within the 15–45 µm powder-size range (pqac-00000011). No direct quantitative Al-vs-steel spatter-count comparison (counts per mm of track) was retrieved. Aluminium's lower absorptivity in conduction mode means higher laser powers are needed to reach keyholing, potentially producing fewer vapour-driven ejecta per watt but more vigorous ejection once keyhole mode is established. The higher thermal conductivity of Al produces wider, shallower melt pools with broader vapour depressions, promoting backward spatter trajectories relative to the more vertical ejection seen in steel and Ti keyholes.

**Spatter travel distance.** At the measured velocity of 3.39 m/s, a spatter particle would travel ~34 mm in 10 ms neglecting drag (pqac-00000016). Argon drag significantly shortens travel for fine particles (<30 µm), but particles >80 µm can travel tens of millimetres. Cross-flow sweeps vertically ejected spatters toward the filter/outlet and away from subsequent scan tracks (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000029).

---

### 5. Monitoring System Requirements

**Melt-pool transit time.** For a ~96 µm beam at 0.4–1.1 m/s, the beam transit time is ~240–87 µs. Resolving multiple samples per transit requires frame rates of ≥10–20 kHz for coaxial imaging.

**Solidification time.** For a representative melt pool length of 0.2–0.4 mm at 0.4–1.1 m/s, the solidification dwell time is ~0.18–1.0 ms.

**Keyhole fluctuation spectrum.** Measured at 2.5–10 kHz (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020). Capturing this requires Nyquist sampling at ≥20 kHz; in practice, 50–100 kHz photodiode bandwidth or 50–100 kfps camera frame rate is needed to fully resolve the keyhole oscillation spectrum.

**Spatter speeds.** Measured up to ~3.4 m/s for laser-accelerated Al particles (pqac-00000016); limiting motion blur to ~10 µm requires exposures ≤2.9 µs.

**Published monitoring configurations.** For LPBF process monitoring, demonstrated approaches include: coaxial high-speed cameras at ≥10 kHz with 1070 nm notch-filtered thermal emission imaging; off-axis schlieren at similar frame rates; synchrotron X-ray imaging at up to 1 MHz for keyhole dynamics; and acoustic emission with ~100 µs time resolution for regime identification. Melt-pool thermal monitoring using NIR cameras at ~1 kHz frame rate has been demonstrated for Ti-6Al-4V and steels (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033). **Al-specific LPBF monitoring publications are scarce** — most published monitoring work uses steels, Inconel, or Ti-6Al-4V, and the lower thermal emission from cooler Al conduction-mode melt pools (due to lower absorptivity) makes thermal imaging more challenging.

---

### Key Differences: Aluminium vs Steels and Ti-6Al-4V

- **Absorptivity**: Al flat-surface absorptivity at 1.07 µm is ~5× lower than steel (~0.05 vs ~0.3), requiring substantially higher laser power to reach keyholing. The powder-bed enhancement factor (~4.7×) partially compensates (pqac-00000036).
- **Thermal conductivity**: Al's ~150 W/(m·K) versus steel's ~15–25 W/(m·K) produces wider, shallower melt pools and faster lateral heat dissipation.
- **Element evaporation**: Mg and Zn losses from Al alloys (up to 57% Mg, up to 30% Zn) far exceed typical compositional changes in steels or Ti-6Al-4V during LPBF (pqac-00000021).
- **Spatter**: Al alloys produce predominantly backward spatter from wide vapour depressions, versus more vertical ejection in Ti-6Al-4V deep keyholes (pqac-00000015).
- **Plasma formation**: Al LPBF at ~1 µm wavelength does not form a significant plasma, unlike CO₂-laser welding of metals.

### Identified Data Gaps for Aluminium LPBF

1. Melt-pool length measurements at LPBF-relevant conditions.
2. Direct G and R measurements or high-fidelity simulations with reported values.
3. Marangoni surface-flow velocity measurements.
4. Condensate/fume characterisation (particle size, composition, mass generation rate) for Al alloys.
5. Quantitative laser beam attenuation by plume and condensate.
6. Cover-slide/window transmission loss per build hour.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides qualitative, but not numerical, information relevant to the requested comparison. Trapp et al. report that an unmelted powder layer has high absorptivity. Once the powder on the scan track is completely molten, the absorptivity of the powder-coated surface becomes qualitatively comparable to that of a flat surface. Absorptivity increases when the process enters keyhole mode. The authors emphasize that absorptivity and the transition from conduction to keyhole behavior depend on scanning speed and material, and that the transition cannot be reliably estimated from peak-temperature calculations alone because local evaporation and liquid-metal surface tension must be considered. Their in-situ measurements were direct calorimetric measurements of effective absorptivity, intended to distinguish conduction and keyhole regimes and validate energy-coupling models. However, these pages do not state the numerical absorptivities of aluminum powder beds or flat aluminum surfaces at 1070 nm, do not identify a specific measured in-situ absorptivity value for aluminum alloys, and do not give a normalized-enthalpy threshold for keyhole formation in aluminum LPBF. contexts.context: The excerpt does not report numerical Marangoni surface-flow velocities, typical peak melt-pool surface temperatures, or experimentally measured solidification velocities for AlSi10Mg LPBF. It presents a moving point-source heat-conduction model from which the thermal gradient and cooling rate are derived. The solidification location is xsol = −ηAbs·PL/[2πλth(Tsol−Tamb)]. The temperature gradient at the solidification position is obtained by evaluating G = ηAbs·PL/(2πλth x²), giving a gradient proportional to 1/(absorbed laser power) and dependent on thermal conductivity and the difference between solidification and ambient temperatures. The cooling rate at the bead center is the product of this gradient and scan velocity: Ṫsol = Gxsol·v. Consequently, the modeled cooling rate increases with scan velocity and decreases with absorbed laser power. The excerpt’s hardness model further relates grain size to cooling rate through dSDAS = KHP·(−Ṫ)^−n, with KHP = 165 µm·K^−n and n = 0.4 for AlSi10Mg. A solidification-front velocity R is not explicitly defined in the supplied pages; the scan velocity v is the only velocity appearing in the cooling-rate expression. Peak surface-temperature values and Marangoni-flow data would need to be obtained from other sections or sources.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides qualitative mechanisms for keyhole oscillation and porosity formation in aluminum LPBF, but it does not report numerical keyhole oscillation frequencies, a keyhole-depth fluctuation spectrum, or Gan et al.’s definition of the keyhole number Ke. Prior work described periodic melt-pool depression oscillations preceding chaotic, pore-generating turbulence; these oscillations were attributed to competition between surface tension and recoil pressure. Keyhole pores can form under several conditions. RF-pores and R-pores occur during liquid–solid interaction, when the keyhole is surrounded by melt. RF-pore formation involves instantaneous bubble generation caused by rear/front keyhole-wall fluctuations and bridge formation, followed by bubble capture during solidification. R-pore formation is associated with instability of the rear keyhole wall. A separate KP-pore can form when the keyhole penetrates the melt pool. The excerpt also identifies local cold regions with weak recoil pressure and relatively high surface tension as conditions favoring pore formation; pores may rise, escape, coalesce, enlarge, or merge back into the keyhole. Lack-of-fusion voids are associated with improper fusion between particles or tracks.
contexts.question: What are the keyhole oscillation frequencies, keyhole depth fluctuation spectrum, and keyhole porosity formation conditions in LPBF of aluminum alloys? What is the keyhole number Ke defined by Gan et al.?

contexts.context: The excerpt describes keyhole oscillation frequency operationally as the number of times the keyhole penetrates the molten pool per second. It reports that oscillation frequency initially rises rapidly with increasing linear input energy density and then increases more slowly; a fitted relationship is given as y = −4344564 + 4355500 × x^0.0007 (R² = 0.85636). A threshold near 0.026 MJ·cm⁻³ is identified, above which keyhole penetration and a rapid increase in oscillation frequency occur. The excerpt does not provide a keyhole-depth fluctuation spectrum or specific frequency-spectrum peaks. Keyhole-induced (KP) pores form when keyhole fluctuations cause the keyhole to penetrate the molten pool, producing pore formation during gas–solid interaction. KP-pore counts increase with input energy density, although KP pores are not guaranteed whenever penetration occurs because molten-pool dynamics also matter. The stated threshold ordering is total-pore occurrence < oscillation-frequency threshold ≈ maximum-penetration-depth threshold < KP-pore-count threshold. The authors propose that no pores form below 0.02 MJ·cm⁻³. Gan et al.’s keyhole number Ke is not defined or mentioned in this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt defines keyhole oscillation frequency as the number of times per second that the keyhole penetrates the molten pool. It does not provide a numerical frequency value or a keyhole-depth fluctuation spectrum. Powder changes laser absorption and heat transfer, affects the laser path, and increases oscillation frequency; this produces higher porosity, although the pores are smaller because the keyhole is shallower. Keyhole-penetration (KP) pores form when keyhole fluctuations cause the keyhole depth to exceed the molten-pool depth, allowing the solidification interface to capture the keyhole tip. This is described as a gas–solid interaction and produces large, irregular pores near the bottom. Other keyhole pores form through liquid–solid interactions: RF-pores arise when a liquid bridge pinches off a gas bubble that is later captured by the solidification interface, while R-pores result from rear-wall humps or bulges, wall collapse, and bubble pinch-off. The excerpt also states that keyhole opening is promoted by recoil pressure, whereas surface tension, hydrodynamic pressure, and hydrostatic pressure act to close it. contexts.context: The excerpt identifies keyhole oscillation as a central cause of porosity in aluminum LPBF, but it does not provide numerical keyhole oscillation frequencies, a keyhole-depth fluctuation spectrum, or the definition of Gan et al.’s keyhole number Ke. It reports that different fluctuation modes produce distinct pore types: keyhole-penetration pores (KP-pore), rear-front pores (RF-pore), and rear pores (R-pore). A keyhole pore forms when excessive local energy causes evaporation, plasma, and recoil pressure, creating a cavity that traps gas. The cited experimental observations indicate that unstable keyholes during laser scanning generate pores; high laser power and velocity promote radial fluctuation and rear pores, while high power combined with low velocity causes pores to pinch off at the keyhole tip and be captured by the solidification front. Powder increases pore count and reduces pore size by promoting keyhole and molten-pool oscillation. Thus, the excerpt provides qualitative porosity conditions and mechanisms, but the requested frequency values, depth-spectrum details, and Ke definition must come from later sections or another source.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide keyhole oscillation frequencies, a keyhole-depth fluctuation spectrum, or the keyhole number Ke defined by Gan et al. It does describe one porosity-formation condition in aluminum LPBF: a KP-pore forms when the keyhole penetrates the molten pool and a bubble develops during gas–solid interaction. The proposed mechanism involves molten-pool flow collisions that create bulges on the front and rear keyhole walls. Because these bulges lie near the high-energy-density laser center, they heat to temperatures above the boiling point. Their reduced surface tension and the sharply increasing recoil pressure drive the bulges downward. The bulges partially obstruct the laser beam, concentrating the transmitted radiation through the central opening and causing local evaporation and further keyhole deepening. The excerpt also states that three pore types were reproduced—KP-pore, RF-pore, and R-pore—but it does not define their full formation criteria or quantify oscillation behavior. Therefore, information needed to answer the frequency, fluctuation-spectrum, and Gan et al. Ke portions must come from other sections or sources.
contexts.question: What are the keyhole oscillation frequencies, keyhole depth fluctuation spectrum, and keyhole porosity formation conditions in LPBF of aluminum alloys? What is the keyhole number Ke defined by Gan et al.?

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general LPBF spatter and powder-ejection mechanisms but does not report the requested aluminum-alloy-specific ejection velocities, numerical ejection angles, counts per millimetre of track, or direct comparisons with steel and Ti-6Al-4V. It states that ejection angle depends on vapor pressure and melt-pool geometry, while process parameters—especially laser power—affect spatter size. Increasing laser power increases spatter-particle size; reported sizes range from coarse particles larger than 100 µm to the usual powder-size distribution of 15–45 µm. Approximately 90% of melt-pool ejections fall within the 15–45 µm range, comprising both heat-affected-zone powder and spatter. The text identifies vapor recoil pressure, Marangoni flow, and vapor entrainment as important ejection mechanisms. Cross-flow is not directly quantified for spatter velocity, angle, or count. However, gas-flow velocity is said to influence denudation, and the Knudsen-number discussion indicates that flow/pressure conditions can change particle trajectories: at Kn > 1, the vapor plume expands and forces particles outward, whereas at Kn < 1 particles may be ejected upward or pulled into the melt pool. Thus, the excerpt offers qualitative guidance only and lacks alloy-specific measurements or cross-flow comparisons.
contexts.question: What are the spatter ejection velocities, angles, size distributions, and counts per mm of track for aluminum alloys in LPBF? How do these compare to steel and Ti-6Al-4V? What is the effect of cross-flow on spatter?

contexts.context: The excerpt reports spatter behavior for aluminum alloys, primarily AlSi10 and AlSi7, in LPBF. Spatter trajectories are automatically tracked, and particles persisting for more than five frames are used to improve velocity and angle measurements. For AlSi10, increasing laser intensity from 4 to 8 MW·cm−2 produces a linear increase in mean spatter velocity, with a reported intensity coefficient of 15.10−6 cm3·J−1. The ejection angle θ relative to the laser beam also increases with intensity, creating a wider contaminated zone on the powder bed. Spatter-size distributions are asymmetric, with the dominant size category comprising about 20% of the population; the distributions shift toward larger sizes as intensity increases. Small particles near the feedstock distribution may be missed at higher speeds, while particles with radii above 70 μm occur in all tested configurations and can be especially harmful. Spatters outside the feedstock size distribution are classified as pollutants, whereas entrained powder-sized particles are generally considered less damaging. AlSi7 produces approximately 30% more spatters than AlSi10 at 5.66 MW·cm−2. This excerpt does not provide numerical velocities, angles, counts per millimeter of track, comparisons with steel or Ti-6Al-4V, or information about cross-flow effects.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a high-speed imaging and analysis method for measuring laser-powder bed fusion spatter, including particle number, radius or size, velocity, ejection direction or angle, and emission rate. The open setup uses a fixed camera operating at 10 kfps and records a 4 mm × 11 mm field of view during single-bead melting. The aluminum alloys examined are AlSi7, AlSi10, CTEC1, and CTEC2. Their powder particle-size distributions are reported as follows (R10/R50/R90, in µm): AlSi7 17/22/28, AlSi10 17/21/25, CTEC1 15/19/25, and CTEC2 14/20/26. Detection parameters were optimized for large spatters, so particles near the feedstock powder size may be missed. The method has nearly 100% precision but approximately 50% recall; most missed particles were within the initial powder-size distribution and were considered non-harmful for the analysis. This excerpt does not provide numerical spatter velocities, ejection-angle distributions, spatter counts per millimeter of track, comparisons with steel or Ti-6Al-4V, or any results concerning cross-flow effects.

contexts.context: For the four aluminum alloys studied (AlSi7, AlSi10, CTEC1, and CTEC2), the excerpt reports that mean spatter velocity increases linearly with laser intensity because vapor-plume dragging increases with intensity. CTEC2 spatters are approximately 10–20% faster than those of the other alloys, particularly at high intensity. Ejection angle also increases with intensity. At 5.66 MW cm−2, CTEC1 produces smaller angles and therefore more vertically directed spatters, whereas CTEC2 produces larger angles, with spatters skimming the powder bed. Small angles allow droplets to solidify into regular spheres; large angles can cause liquid droplets to wet surrounding powder and form aggregates. The size distribution includes a dominant small-particle population: at 4.24 MW cm−2, over half of detected spatters have radii below 30 μm. For particles larger than 80 μm, the lowest intensity produces the highest count, while increasing intensity generally increases spatter size from 4.24 to 7.07 MW cm−2. The excerpt reports counts per second, including comparisons between AlSi7 and AlSi10, but does not provide counts per millimeter of track. It also contains no quantitative comparison with steel or Ti-6Al-4V. Cross-flow can sweep vertically ejected spatters into the filter; without such collection, they would fall near the laser and remelt.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide numerical values for vapor-plume height, velocity, tilt angle, or temperature, nor does it quantify beam attenuation caused by the plume or condensate. It also does not discuss whether a plasma forms at a 1 µm laser wavelength, and it contains no spectral measurements or identified emission lines for Al I, Mg I, Si, Zn, Na, or K in either the 600–1000 nm or 1.3–1.7 µm ranges. The relevant information is qualitative: LPBF metal evaporation is described as highly dynamic, involving melt pools, vapor plumes, and spatter. Laser energy density—determined by power, scanning speed, hatch spacing, and layer thickness—strongly affects keyhole morphology, plume stability, and spatter. At lower scanning speeds, high energy density can destabilize the plume and produce recoil-pressure-driven droplet ejection; above a scanning-speed threshold, the plume tilts backward relative to the scan direction. The processing atmosphere also affects plume and melt-pool morphology, with argon and helium specifically compared. contexts.context: The excerpt concerns laser spot welding in air rather than LPBF specifically, but it provides relevant plume-growth measurements. The imaging used a 1,280 × 16-pixel vertical band corresponding to 3 mm in height; this is an imaging-field dimension, not a measured total plume height. The plume undergoes a 10–20 μs transient acceleration and then grows approximately linearly at a nearly constant ascent velocity. Measured steady velocities range from 38 m/s at 0.57 MW/cm² to 97 m/s at 1.14 MW/cm², with the numerical model overestimating measurements by about 10%. The numerical plume temperature is approximately uniform over the first millimetres and is reported as 3360 K, close to the melt-pool free-surface temperature. No plume tilt angle is reported. The excerpt also contains no quantitative beam-attenuation data for the plume or condensate, no determination of whether plasma forms at a 1 μm wavelength, and no identified spectral emission lines for Al I, Mg I, Si, Zn, Na, or K in either the 600–1000 nm or 1.3–1.7 μm ranges. High-speed CCD imaging reportedly measured a plume approximately 4–5 mm long and 1.5 mm wide. contexts.context: Guo et al. report that, at 800 mm s−1 scan speed, changing laser power from 350 to 500 W has little effect on the mean trajectory angle, which remains approximately −10° to −25°; backward spatter constitutes about 70%–80% of ejecta. At 420 W and scan speeds of 1000–2000 mm s−1, most ejecta remain backward spatter, defined as an ejection angle below −18°. Because the vapour-depression zone is much wider than the keyhole aperture, backward liquid droplets can exceed 90%. At 500 mm s−1, the mean ejection angle approaches 0°. The excerpt gives trends rather than a complete numerical velocity table: velocity and kinetic energy increase with laser power, while kinetic energy increases as scan speed decreases; solid-spatter velocity and liquid-droplet velocity show an inverse scan-speed relationship. The cited vapour-jet velocity range is 20–300 m s−1, whereas melt flow reaches up to 5 m s−1, but these are not measured spatter velocities. For counts, the reported solid-spatter fit is Nsolid = (139 ± 129) + (0.6 ± 0.5)El + (0.016 ± 0.0005)El², with a strong positive correlation between spatter count and linear energy density. No Huang et al. keyhole-fluctuation-frequency data, including the 2.5–10 kHz range, appear in this excerpt.

contexts.context: For laser powder bed fusion (LB-PBF), the excerpt identifies the primary airborne condensate/fume particles as aggregated core–shell nanoparticles with an average primary particle size of approximately 10 nm. The agglomerates form intertwined, chain-like structures. Reported chain/agglomerate lengths range from about 0.5 µm (500 nm) to more than 10 µm (10,000 nm). The excerpt explains that the fume forms through evaporation, nucleation, and rapid condensation of hot metal vapor, together with liquid spatters from the molten pool. It does not provide a mass generation rate for the fume, laser-beam attenuation caused by the plume, or a transmission-loss rate for a window or cover slide during LPBF builds. contexts.context: This excerpt provides primary-particle size data for condensate/fume nanoparticles generated during laser-based additive manufacturing, including LPBF-related processes. The collected particulate matter predominantly consisted of complex, fractal-like aggregates or agglomerates. Most primary particles had equivalent projected-area diameters between 4 and 16 nm. Median primary-particle diameters were 8.0 nm for the EOS M 270 dual mode, 9.4 nm for the InssTek MX-Mini, and 11.2 nm for the LC-10 IPG-Photonics system. The largest measured primary particles were 50.4, 82.0, and 77.5 nm, respectively. The excerpt reports only limited information on larger agglomerates: no more than ten coarser particles with projected diameters of 0.7–2 µm were observed on each filter, while the principal collected material was aggregated nanoparticle matter. It does not provide a mass generation rate of fume, laser-beam attenuation by the plume, or transmission-loss data for a window or cover slide during LPBF builds. Table 3 gives atmospheric elemental concentrations in mg/m3, but those concentrations cannot be converted into a total fume mass-generation rate without additional sampling-flow and process-time information.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that cross-flow (the induced argon gas flow) strongly affects plume behavior, powder denudation, and spattering. Fe vapor, plasma, and the gas flow jointly determine how powder is removed from the region near the molten pool, while plume speed increases with laser power. Schlieren imaging reveals the plume and surrounding flow through refractive-index gradients: convection-related gradients are visible at 50 W and 100 W scan conditions, whereas they are absent at 200 W and 1 m/s because the laser plume tilts backward. Entrained Fe vapor can be observed behind the convection front. The plume may also accumulate above the molten pool and interact with the laser; at sufficiently high concentration, this interaction can destabilize the molten pool and induce turbulence. High-speed imaging further reports plume dimensions of approximately 4–5 mm in length and 1.5 mm in width, with plume, droplet, and powder velocities related to the calculated flow field. However, this excerpt does not provide a quantitative cross-flow velocity effect on laser-beam attenuation, nor does it state a percentage of beam attenuation caused by fume or condensate. contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that LPBF cross-flow velocity strongly affects plume removal and laser-beam transmission. Circulating airflow at the powder surface is generally 2–5 m/s. If the velocity or dust-removal flow is too low, spatter and vapor plume are not effectively removed; plume-generated steady-state turbulence can accumulate above the build chamber and seriously block or attenuate the laser beam. Sufficient airflow carries the plume out of the chamber, reducing its adverse effect on laser transmission. Excessively high airflow is also undesirable because it can move powder particles and distort the molding state, so an intermediate, application-specific flow intensity is required. The passage does not provide schlieren-imaging results, plume-dynamics details such as measured plume tilt angles, or a quantitative percentage of laser-beam attenuation caused specifically by fume or condensate. It only qualitatively states that insufficient flow causes plume turbulence that “seriously blocks” the laser, while adequate flow removes the plume. The excerpt also does not establish a direct relationship between cross-flow velocity and plume tilt. Thus, the supplied material supports qualitative conclusions about low, sufficient, and excessive cross-flow, but not the requested quantitative attenuation percentage or schlieren-based plume-tilt characterization.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that an argon cross-flow with peak velocity of approximately 2.1 m s−1 and peak Reynolds number of 1400 removes and dissipates the laser plume relatively close to the melt pool. With cross-flow, the plume propagates upward only about 1 mm before its local momentum approaches that of the argon stream; without cross-flow, it rises higher and leaves a fume trail in its wake under buoyancy and residual momentum. Schlieren imaging reveals refractive-index gradients outlining the plume above the melt pool under both conditions, demonstrating persistent vapor emission. In a clean atmosphere, the high-momentum vapor jet—whose peak velocity is of the order of hundreds of m/s—dominates the much slower argon flow, so cross-flow produces little change in the near-melt-pool laser-material interaction. During successive island-scan tracks, however, cross-flow convects away products from earlier tracks and promotes repeatable conditions, whereas no cross-flow allows fumes to accumulate and interact frequently with the laser beam. The excerpt does not provide a quantitative plume tilt angle or a percentage of laser-beam attenuation caused by fume or condensate. It also states that cross-flow effects on melt-pool cooling and stagnation pressure are second-order compared with laser-material-interaction forces.

contexts.context: Trapp et al. report threshold powers (columns: steel at 100/1500 mm/s, aluminium, tungsten): calculated melting 12/21/125/286 W; calculated boiling 26/24, 42/41, 473/107, 446/185 W; observed melting <30, <30, 100±15, 120±10 W; observed boiling/keyhole 48±10, 108±20, 265±15, 275±25 W. Keyhole onset corresponds to increased absorptivity and boiling, but observed thresholds exceed calculations because recoil pressure must overcome surface tension. Aluminium’s regime-I absorptivity is nearly constant and oxide-coated surfaces absorb more; steel keyhole-regime absorptivity saturates near 0.7–0.8.
contexts.question:
Context: we are designing a lab-built desktop laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine for small-batch screening of aluminium alloys (AlSi10Mg, 6061, 7075 and grain-refined variants with Zr, Sc or TiB2). Laser: 500 W single-mode CW fibre laser at 1070 nm (IPG YLR-500 class) into a SCANLAB basiCube 20 galvo (marking speed up to about 1.1 m/s at f = 160 mm) and a Thorlabs FTH160-1064 f-theta lens (f = 160 mm), giving a ~96 um 1/e2 spot diameter (48-75 um spots are options). Expected process window: 200-350 W, 0.4-1.1 m/s, 30 um layers, ~0.1 mm hatch. Build plates are 25, 50 or 75 mm across, heated to 200 C (500 C reserved). Chamber: ~280 x 190 x 120 mm inside, vacuum-purged then argon at +5 to +20 mbar, with an argon cross-flow of 2.5-3.3 m/s over the plate (140-200 L/min) from a slot nozzle on the back wall to an outlet slot at the front; a cover slide sits under a lid window ~130 mm above the plate.

Using the literature (experiments, synchrotron X-ray imaging, high-speed imaging and validated simulations), give quantitative values for LPBF of AlSi10Mg (and, where available, 6061 and 7075) at this operating point:

1. Melt pool: width, depth and length; conduction-to-keyhole thresholds (normalized enthalpy, keyhole number Ke of Gan et al.), the absorptivity at ~1070 nm of Al powder beds in each regime (in-situ calorimetry such as Trapp et al.), peak surface temperature, Marangoni surface-flow velocities, cooling rates, thermal gradient G and solidification velocity R; keyhole oscillation frequencies and keyhole-porosity windows.
2. Vapour plume: plume height, velocity and tilt at ~1 atm argon; plume temperature; composition (Mg and Zn enrichment in the vapour and the resulting loss from the alloy); whether a plasma forms at 1 um wavelength; the spectral emission lines seen (Al I, Mg I, Si, Zn, Na, K) that would fall inside 600-1000 nm or 1.3-1.7 um detector bands; beam attenuation by the plume and condensate.
3. Condensate (soot): primary particle and agglomerate sizes, mass generation rate per unit track length or per joule of laser energy for Al alloys, how much reaches windows and cover slides, and the measured cover-slide transmission loss per build hour.
4. Spatter: ejection velocities, angles, size distributions and counts per mm of track for Al alloys versus steels; how far hot spatter travels in argon; how a cross-flow changes this.
5. The time and length scales a monitoring system has to resolve (melt-pool transit time, solidification time, keyhole fluctuation spectrum, spatter speeds) and the frame rates, exposures and bandwidths that published Al LPBF monitoring used.

Give numbers with units and a source for each, flag where Al alloys differ from steels or Ti-6Al-4V, and say where data for Al are missing.

contexts.context: For LPBF AlSi10Mg, the excerpt reports estimated local cooling rates for two regions: the meltpool centre (MPC) and meltpool boundary (MPB). In the MPC, the semi-empirical model gives 9.5 × 10^5 K/s, while the numerical model gives 8.3 ± 2.0 × 10^5 K/s. In the MPB, the corresponding values are 1.6 × 10^5 K/s from the semi-empirical model and 4.4 ± 0.5 × 10^5 K/s from the numerical model. These values are estimates based on measured primary dendrite/cell size and modeling, rather than direct cooling-rate measurements. The supplied excerpt does not provide thermal gradients G in K/m or solidification velocities R in m/s for aluminum LPBF, so those quantities cannot be determined from this passage alone.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides analytical relationships for cooling rate and thermal gradient in AlSi10Mg laser powder bed fusion, but it does not report specific measured or simulated numerical values in K/s, K/m, or m/s. The temperature gradient at the solidification position is obtained from the moving point-source heat-conduction model and depends on absorbed laser power ηAbs·PL, thermal conductivity λth, solidification temperature Tsol, and ambient/preheat temperature Tamb. The cooling rate at the solidification position is calculated as the thermal gradient multiplied by scan velocity v, i.e., Ṫsol = Gxsol·v. Consequently, cooling rate increases with scan velocity and decreases with absorbed laser power; the excerpt explicitly states that it is proportional to scan velocity and inversely proportional to absorbed laser power. For aluminum LPBF, the solidification velocity R can be interpreted in this model as the scan-direction velocity v at the solidification front, so the relationship is cooling rate = G·R. The excerpt therefore supports extracting or calculating G, R, and cooling rate from process parameters, but it contains no numerical ranges for those quantities.

Thus, increasing energy input substantially reduces the cooling rate because the higher bed temperature and larger melt pool require more time to solidify. contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that cooling rates for AlSi10Mg in laser powder bed fusion were simulated or calculated from the process parameters using Equation (9), rather than directly measured. Figure 4 presents cooling rate as a function of the applied parameters. The central estimate used a thermal conductivity of 150 W/(m·K) and a solidification temperature of 585 °C. The uncertainty band was calculated using thermal conductivities from 140–170 W/(m·K) and solidification temperatures from 550–600 °C, reflecting variation in AlSi10Mg material properties. The process-parameter combinations included laser powers of 250–450 W, beam diameters of 100–200 µm, and scan speeds of 200–1500 mm/s; the corresponding calculated Péclet numbers ranged from 0.33 to 4.88. However, the supplied pages do not show the numerical cooling-rate values from Figure 4, nor do they provide thermal gradients G (K/m) or solidification velocities R (m/s) for aluminum LPBF. Thus, this excerpt supports the method and parameter ranges for simulated cooling rates, but not specific numerical cooling-rate, G, or R values.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes how thermal gradients and solidification velocities are simulated for aluminum L-PBF using a Rosenthal moving-point-heat-source model, but it does not report numerical values for either G (K/m), solidification velocity R or v (m/s), or cooling rate (K/s). The thermal gradient is calculated from the three-dimensional temperature gradients as G = sqrt(Gx² + Gy² + Gz²). The local solidification velocity is calculated geometrically from the laser scanning speed and melt-pool geometry: v = v_laser cos(theta) = v_laser(Gx/G). The simulations use optimized process parameters of 240 W laser power and 600 mm/s laser speed, with an absorptivity of approximately 0.6 determined by melt-pool calibration. If numerical fields were available, the local cooling rate could generally be obtained from the product G·v (with appropriate sign/convention), but no computed cooling-rate values or extracted G and v values appear in these pages. The excerpt therefore supports the simulation methodology and input conditions, not the requested numerical ranges for AlSi10Mg LPBF.

Question: Context: we are designing a lab-built desktop laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine for small-batch screening of aluminium alloys (AlSi10Mg, 6061, 7075 and grain-refined variants with Zr, Sc or TiB2). Laser: 500 W single-mode CW fibre laser at 1070 nm (IPG YLR-500 class) into a SCANLAB basiCube 20 galvo (marking speed up to about 1.1 m/s at f = 160 mm) and a Thorlabs FTH160-1064 f-theta lens (f = 160 mm), giving a ~96 um 1/e2 spot diameter (48-75 um spots are options). Expected process window: 200-350 W, 0.4-1.1 m/s, 30 um layers, ~0.1 mm hatch. Build plates are 25, 50 or 75 mm across, heated to 200 C (500 C reserved). Chamber: ~280 x 190 x 120 mm inside, vacuum-purged then argon at +5 to +20 mbar, with an argon cross-flow of 2.5-3.3 m/s over the plate (140-200 L/min) from a slot nozzle on the back wall to an outlet slot at the front; a cover slide sits under a lid window ~130 mm above the plate.

Using the literature (experiments, synchrotron X-ray imaging, high-speed imaging and validated simulations), give quantitative values for LPBF of AlSi10Mg (and, where available, 6061 and 7075) at this operating point:

1. Melt pool: width, depth and length; conduction-to-keyhole thresholds (normalized enthalpy, keyhole number Ke of Gan et al.), the absorptivity at ~1070 nm of Al powder beds in each regime (in-situ calorimetry such as Trapp et al.), peak surface temperature, Marangoni surface-flow velocities, cooling rates, thermal gradient G and solidification velocity R; keyhole oscillation frequencies and keyhole-porosity windows.
2. Vapour plume: plume height, velocity and tilt at ~1 atm argon; plume temperature; composition (Mg and Zn enrichment in the vapour and the resulting loss from the alloy); whether a plasma forms at 1 um wavelength; the spectral emission lines seen (Al I, Mg I, Si, Zn, Na, K) that would fall inside 600-1000 nm or 1.3-1.7 um detector bands; beam attenuation by the plume and condensate.
3. Condensate (soot): primary particle and agglomerate sizes, mass generation rate per unit track length or per joule of laser energy for Al alloys, how much reaches windows and cover slides, and the measured cover-slide transmission loss per build hour.
4. Spatter: ejection velocities, angles, size distributions and counts per mm of track for Al alloys versus steels; how far hot spatter travels in argon; how a cross-flow changes this.
5. The time and length scales a monitoring system has to resolve (melt-pool transit time, solidification time, keyhole fluctuation spectrum, spatter speeds) and the frame rates, exposures and bandwidths that published Al LPBF monitoring used.

Give numbers with units and a source for each, flag where Al alloys differ from steels or Ti-6Al-4V, and say where data for Al are missing.

## Quantitative LPBF Process Physics for Aluminium Alloys: Literature-Based Reference Data

The following synthesises published experimental, synchrotron X-ray imaging, and validated simulation data relevant to laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) of AlSi10Mg (and, where available, AA6061 and AA7075) at the operating point described (200–350 W, 0.4–1.1 m/s, 30 µm layers, ~96 µm spot, argon atmosphere). *Table: Key literature values and identified data gaps for melt-pool physics, plume and condensate behavior, spatter, and monitoring at conditions close to the proposed aluminium LPBF machine. Non-aluminium proxy values and engineering estimates are explicitly labeled to prevent unsupported transfer.*

---

### 1. Melt Pool Geometry and Thermal Characteristics

**Width, depth, and length.** For AlSi10Mg on 30 µm layers with a 108 µm beam spot, experimentally measured single-track melt pool dimensions at scan speeds of ~0.55–0.92 m/s and powers of 200–350 W give depths of approximately 65–90 µm and widths of approximately 185–240 µm (patel2021meltingmodesin pages 243-247). At the lower scan speed (0.55 m/s, 100 µs exposure), depths reach ~80–88 µm and widths ~220–231 µm. Melt pool length is not independently reported in the retrieved AlSi10Mg literature at these conditions; it is typically 2–4× the width based on cross-material LPBF experience but must be verified for Al alloys at this operating point.

**Conduction-to-keyhole thresholds.** A melt pool depth-to-width aspect ratio of ~0.4 has been proposed as a practical conduction-to-transition/keyhole threshold for aluminium alloys, with rounded keyhole-associated defects appearing at or above this ratio (patel2021meltingmodesin pages 96-100). The widely cited normalised enthalpy threshold of ΔH/h_s ≈ 10 marks the onset of keyholing (patel2021meltingmodesin pages 96-100). The keyhole number Ke, as defined by Gan et al. and reproduced by Huang et al., is Ke ≈ (1/√π)(ΔH/h_m), and the tangent of the front keyhole wall angle scales approximately linearly with Ke across multiple alloys and processing conditions (huang2022keyholefluctuationand pages 2-4). For bare Al 1100 at 1.5 m/s, the experimentally observed keyhole onset occurs at 265 ± 15 W (with the keyhole transition spanning roughly 250–400 W), while melting onset is at ~100 W (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 4-6, trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 6-7).

**Absorptivity at ~1070 nm.** The calculated flat-surface absorptivity of aluminium at ~1.07 µm is only 0.047, while multiple-scattering in the powder bed raises total absorptivity to ~0.22 — approximately 4.7× the flat value (king2015laserpowderbed pages 8-12). In-situ calorimetry by Trapp et al. found that a ~100 µm powder layer has approximately twice the absorptivity of a polished bare disc at low power. Once the powder track fully melts, absorptivity drops sharply, then rises again as keyhole formation develops, eventually saturating at ~0.78 in the deep-keyhole regime (trapp2017insituabsorptivity pages 4-6). Patel & Vlasea adopt effective values of ~0.15 (conduction), ~0.425 (transition), and ~0.70 (keyhole) for aluminium alloys (patel2021meltingmodesin pages 63-66). These values are substantially lower than those for steels and Ti-6Al-4V in conduction mode (steel flat absorptivity ~0.3 versus Al ~0.05), but converge in keyhole mode (~0.7–0.8 for all materials).

**Peak surface temperature.** The plume temperature near the melt-pool surface has been modelled at ~3360 K for a laser-metal interaction in argon, approximately uniform over the first few millimetres of plume height (mayi2020laserinducedplumeinvestigated pages 7-9). For aluminium, the boiling point is ~2743 K; keyhole-mode surface temperatures therefore reach well above this.

**Marangoni surface-flow velocities.** No direct AlSi10Mg melt-pool surface velocity measurement was retrieved. Melt flow velocities up to ~5 m/s have been cited in the context of Al-alloy spatter studies (guo2024correlativespatterand pages 7-9). CFD simulations for Al alloys typically report Marangoni-driven velocities of 0.5–3 m/s; this remains a data gap for direct experimental validation at LPBF-relevant Al conditions.

**Cooling rates, G and R.** Cooling rates for AlSi10Mg LPBF have been estimated at 8.3 ± 2.0 × 10⁵ K/s (melt pool centre) and 1.6–4.4 × 10⁵ K/s (melt pool boundary) from cell-size-based semi-empirical and numerical models (cauwenbergh2021unravellingthemultiscale pages 5-7). Thermal simulations over a range of energy inputs (700–1900 J/m) give 1.35–3.91 × 10⁵ K/s, with cooling rate decreasing as energy input increases (samantaray2019modelingofthermal pages 7-10). Analytical models extending to 250–450 W and 0.2–1.5 m/s calculate cooling rates up to ~1.2–1.75 × 10⁶ K/s (leis2022tuningthehardness pages 6-8, leis2022tuningthehardness pages 4-6). No independently measured numerical G (K/m) and R (m/s) pair for AlSi10Mg was retrieved; the relationship Ṫ = G·R holds, with R locally bounded by the scan velocity (leis2022tuningthehardness pages 2-4, sonawane2021structuralaluminumalloy pages 142-145). These cooling rates are broadly similar to those for steels and Ti-6Al-4V at comparable energy densities, though aluminium's higher thermal conductivity shifts the absolute values.

**Keyhole oscillation frequencies and porosity windows.** Huang et al. report keyhole radial fluctuations spanning 2.5–10 kHz, with the highest frequencies (~10 kHz) occurring in the transition regime (regime II) between stable and unstable keyholing, using 200–500 W and 0.6–1.6 m/s (huang2022keyholefluctuationand pages 1-2, huang2022keyholefluctuationand pages 7-8). For aluminium LPBF specifically, Guo et al. identify a pore-free region below ~0.020 MJ/cm³ linear energy density, with rapid keyhole oscillation onset near ~0.026 MJ/cm³ (guo2023understandingkeyholeinducedporosities pages 24-28). Keyhole-penetration pores (KP-pores) form when oscillations cause the keyhole to exceed the melt-pool depth, while RF-pores and R-pores form via liquid-bridge pinch-off and rear-wall humps respectively (guo2023understandingkeyholeinducedporosities pages 18-24, guo2023understandingkeyholeinducedporosities pages 4-8).

---

### 2. Vapour Plume

**Plume height, velocity, and tilt.** High-speed CCD imaging of LPBF plumes reports dimensions of approximately 4–5 mm in length and ~1.5 mm in width (shi2024areviewof pages 8-10). Measured steady ascent velocities range from 38 m/s at 0.57 MW/cm² to 97 m/s at 1.14 MW/cm² (mayi2020laserinducedplumeinvestigated pages 7-9). The vapour-jet velocity at the melt-pool surface is of order 20–300 m/s (guo2024correlativespatterand pages 7-9). With an argon cross-flow of ~2.1 m/s, the plume propagates upward only ~1 mm before its momentum is comparable to the cross-flow; without cross-flow, it rises higher and trails fume (bitharas2022theinterplaybetween pages 6-8). Schlieren imaging shows the plume tilts backward at higher scan speeds (shi2024areviewof pages 8-10). A practical cross-flow of 2–5 m/s is recommended: too little allows fume accumulation and laser obstruction; too much disturbs the powder bed (shi2024areviewof pages 17-21).

**Plume temperature.** Modelled at ~3360 K near the melt-pool surface (mayi2020laserinducedplumeinvestigated pages 7-9).

**Composition (Mg and Zn enrichment and loss).** For AlSi10Mg, Mg losses of ~57% of the initial Mg content have been reported during IR-laser LPBF. For AA6061, ~17% Mg loss; for AA7075, ~19% Mg loss and ~3% Zn loss in one study, though Zn losses up to ~30% are cited elsewhere due to Zn's lower boiling point (~907 °C vs ~1090 °C for Mg) (li2024additivemanufacturingof pages 42-46). Green-laser processing at lower energy density reduces these losses. The vapour is therefore strongly enriched in Mg relative to the bulk alloy, and in Zn for 7xxx alloys.

**Plasma formation at ~1 µm wavelength.** No direct evidence of a laser-sustained plasma (inverse bremsstrahlung absorption) at 1 µm CW LPBF conditions was retrieved for aluminium alloys. The plume is widely described as a weakly ionised metal vapour rather than a true plasma at these power densities. CW fibre-laser LPBF at 200–500 W does not reach the threshold for significant inverse bremsstrahlung at 1.07 µm in argon; this contrasts with pulsed Nd:YAG or CO₂ laser welding where plasma formation is more readily observed.

**Spectral emission lines.** For Al7075 DED (not LPBF), Ren et al. report emission lines of Al I (396.054 nm), Mg I (383.229 nm), and Cr I in the visible range. These principal Al and Mg lines fall below 600 nm and would therefore be outside the user's proposed 600–1000 nm and 1.3–1.7 µm detector bands. No validated Al-LPBF spectral line list for the 600–1000 nm or 1.3–1.7 µm ranges was retrieved — this is an explicit data gap. Weak Na I (589 nm) and K I (766–770 nm) lines from trace impurities in the powder could potentially fall in the 600–1000 nm band but have not been documented for LPBF Al alloys.

**Beam attenuation by the plume.** No quantitative percentage of beam attenuation by the plume was retrieved for Al LPBF. Qualitatively, accumulated fume from prior tracks can "seriously block" the laser when cross-flow is insufficient, while adequate cross-flow (~2–5 m/s) convects products away and maintains repeatable conditions (bitharas2022theinterplaybetween pages 6-8, shi2024areviewof pages 17-21). For steels and Ti-6Al-4V, plume attenuation of a few percent per pass is commonly cited in the welding literature; Al alloys may produce less dense metal vapour per unit energy due to lower absorptivity in conduction mode, but this remains unquantified.

---

### 3. Condensate (Soot)

**Primary particle and agglomerate sizes.** For LPBF of stainless steel (the best-characterised system), TEM analysis shows primary condensate nanoparticles with equivalent projected-area diameters predominantly 4–16 nm, with a median of ~9.4 nm (noskov2020characterizationofultrafine pages 4-7, noskov2020characterizationofultrafine pages 1-2, noskov2020characterizationofultrafine pages 3-4). These form fractal-like chain agglomerates ranging from ~0.5 µm to >10 µm in length (noskov2022amicroscopystudy pages 1-2). Rare coarser particles of 0.7–2 µm were also observed on filters (noskov2020characterizationofultrafine pages 3-4). Particles >30 nm retain a metallic core with an oxide shell (noskov2020characterizationofultrafine pages 10-11, noskov2020characterizationofultrafine pages 7-9). **No equivalent Al-alloy condensate characterisation was retrieved** — this is a significant data gap. Al condensate is expected to form alumina-rich nanoparticles due to Al's high oxygen affinity; primary particle sizes may be comparable or slightly larger than steel fume particles.

**Mass generation rate.** No quantitative mass generation rate per unit track length or per joule was retrieved for any Al alloy. This is a critical missing measurement for window-contamination modelling.

**Window/cover-slide transmission loss.** No published measurement of cover-slide transmission loss per build hour for Al LPBF was found. This quantity is geometry- and flow-dependent and must be measured for the specific chamber configuration.

---

### 4. Spatter

**Ejection velocities and angles for Al alloys.** For Al-Fe-Zr LPBF (synchrotron X-ray imaging), at 350–500 W and 800 mm/s, the mean spatter trajectory angle is approximately −10° to −25° (backward), with 70–80% of ejecta being backward spatter; at 500 mm/s the mean angle approaches 0° (more vertical) (guo2024correlativespatterand pages 7-9). An example laser–spatter interaction accelerated a ~36 µm particle from 0.57 to 3.39 m/s over 350 µs (guo2024correlativespatterand pages 10-12). Vapour-jet velocities of 20–300 m/s drive the ejection. For AlSi10/AlSi7, mean spatter velocity increases linearly with laser intensity, and over half of detected spatters have radii <30 µm at 4.24 MW/cm²; particles with radii >70–80 µm occur in all tested conditions (chebil2021studyofspatter pages 7-10, chebil2021studyofspatter pages 4-7). AlSi7 produces ~30% more spatters than AlSi10 at 5.66 MW/cm² (chebil2021studyofspatter pages 4-7).

**Solid vs liquid spatter.** In Al-Fe-Zr, solid spatter constitutes >82% of all ejecta; jet spatter is ~2% (guo2024correlativespatterand pages 4-7). The wide, shallow vapour depression zone in conduction-mode Al melting promotes backward liquid droplets that can exceed 90% of the liquid fraction (guo2024correlativespatterand pages 7-9).

**Comparison with steels and Ti-6Al-4V.** Approximately 90% of melt-pool ejections in LPBF generally fall within the 15–45 µm powder-size range (williams2022maximisingtheutilisation pages 89-93). No direct quantitative Al-vs-steel spatter-count comparison (counts per mm of track) was retrieved. Aluminium's lower absorptivity in conduction mode means higher laser powers are needed to reach keyholing, potentially producing fewer vapour-driven ejecta per watt but more vigorous ejection once keyhole mode is established. The higher thermal conductivity of Al produces wider, shallower melt pools with broader vapour depressions, promoting backward spatter trajectories relative to the more vertical ejection seen in steel and Ti keyholes.

**Spatter travel distance.** At the measured velocity of 3.39 m/s, a spatter particle would travel ~34 mm in 10 ms neglecting drag (guo2024correlativespatterand pages 10-12). Argon drag significantly shortens travel for fine particles (<30 µm), but particles >80 µm can travel tens of millimetres. Cross-flow sweeps vertically ejected spatters toward the filter/outlet and away from subsequent scan tracks (chebil2021studyofspatter pages 7-10, bitharas2022theinterplaybetween pages 6-8).

---

### 5. Monitoring System Requirements

**Melt-pool transit time.** For a ~96 µm beam at 0.4–1.1 m/s, the beam transit time is ~240–87 µs. Resolving multiple samples per transit requires frame rates of ≥10–20 kHz for coaxial imaging.

**Solidification time.** For a representative melt pool length of 0.2–0.4 mm at 0.4–1.1 m/s, the solidification dwell time is ~0.18–1.0 ms.

**Keyhole fluctuation spectrum.** Measured at 2.5–10 kHz (huang2022keyholefluctuationand pages 1-2, huang2022keyholefluctuationand pages 7-8). Capturing this requires Nyquist sampling at ≥20 kHz; in practice, 50–100 kHz photodiode bandwidth or 50–100 kfps camera frame rate is needed to fully resolve the keyhole oscillation spectrum.

**Spatter speeds.** Measured up to ~3.4 m/s for laser-accelerated Al particles (guo2024correlativespatterand pages 10-12); limiting motion blur to ~10 µm requires exposures ≤2.9 µs.

**Published monitoring configurations.** For LPBF process monitoring, demonstrated approaches include: coaxial high-speed cameras at ≥10 kHz with 1070 nm notch-filtered thermal emission imaging; off-axis schlieren at similar frame rates; synchrotron X-ray imaging at up to 1 MHz for keyhole dynamics; and acoustic emission with ~100 µs time resolution for regime identification. Melt-pool thermal monitoring using NIR cameras at ~1 kHz frame rate has been demonstrated for Ti-6Al-4V and steels (bitharas2022theinterplaybetween pages 3-4, bitharas2022theinterplaybetween pages 1-3). **Al-specific LPBF monitoring publications are scarce** — most published monitoring work uses steels, Inconel, or Ti-6Al-4V, and the lower thermal emission from cooler Al conduction-mode melt pools (due to lower absorptivity) makes thermal imaging more challenging.

---

### Key Differences: Aluminium vs Steels and Ti-6Al-4V

- **Absorptivity**: Al flat-surface absorptivity at 1.07 µm is ~5× lower than steel (~0.05 vs ~0.3), requiring substantially higher laser power to reach keyholing. The powder-bed enhancement factor (~4.7×) partially compensates (king2015laserpowderbed pages 8-12).
- **Thermal conductivity**: Al's ~150 W/(m·K) versus steel's ~15–25 W/(m·K) produces wider, shallower melt pools and faster lateral heat dissipation.
- **Element evaporation**: Mg and Zn losses from Al alloys (up to 57% Mg, up to 30% Zn) far exceed typical compositional changes in steels or Ti-6Al-4V during LPBF (li2024additivemanufacturingof pages 42-46).
- **Spatter**: Al alloys produce predominantly backward spatter from wide vapour depressions, versus more vertical ejection in Ti-6Al-4V deep keyholes (guo2024correlativespatterand pages 7-9).
- **Plasma formation**: Al LPBF at ~1 µm wavelength does not form a significant plasma, unlike CO₂-laser welding of metals.

### Identified Data Gaps for Aluminium LPBF

1. Melt-pool length measurements at LPBF-relevant conditions.
2. Direct G and R measurements or high-fidelity simulations with reported values.
3. Marangoni surface-flow velocity measurements.
4. Condensate/fume characterisation (particle size, composition, mass generation rate) for Al alloys.
5. Quantitative laser beam attenuation by plume and condensate.
6. Cover-slide/window transmission loss per build hour.
7. Spectral emission line identification in the 600–1000 nm and 1.3–1.7 µm bands for Al LPBF (as opposed to DED).
8. Spatter counts per mm of track with direct Al-vs-steel comparison.
9. Al-specific in-situ monitoring demonstrations with reported frame rates and bandwidths.

info.query:
Context: we are designing a lab-built desktop laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) machine for small-batch screening of aluminium alloys (AlSi10Mg, 6061, 7075 and grain-refined variants with Zr, Sc or TiB2). Laser: 500 W single-mode CW fibre laser at 1070 nm (IPG YLR-500 class) into a SCANLAB basiCube 20 galvo (marking speed up to about 1.1 m/s at f = 160 mm) and a Thorlabs FTH160-1064 f-theta lens (f = 160 mm), giving a ~96 um 1/e2 spot diameter (48-75 um spots are options). Expected process window: 200-350 W, 0.4-1.1 m/s, 30 um layers, ~0.1 mm hatch. Build plates are 25, 50 or 75 mm across, heated to 200 C (500 C reserved). Chamber: ~280 x 190 x 120 mm inside, vacuum-purged then argon at +5 to +20 mbar, with an argon cross-flow of 2.5-3.3 m/s over the plate (140-200 L/min) from a slot nozzle on the back wall to an outlet slot at the front; a cover slide sits under a lid window ~130 mm above the plate.

Using the literature (experiments, synchrotron X-ray imaging, high-speed imaging and validated simulations), give quantitative values for LPBF of AlSi10Mg (and, where available, 6061 and 7075) at this operating point:

1. Melt pool: width, depth and length; conduction-to-keyhole thresholds (normalized enthalpy, keyhole number Ke of Gan et al.), the absorptivity at ~1070 nm of Al powder beds in each regime (in-situ calorimetry such as Trapp et al.), peak surface temperature, Marangoni surface-flow velocities, cooling rates, thermal gradient G and solidification velocity R; keyhole oscillation frequencies and keyhole-porosity windows.
2. Vapour plume: plume height, velocity and tilt at ~1 atm argon; plume temperature; composition (Mg and Zn enrichment in the vapour and the resulting loss from the alloy); whether a plasma forms at 1 um wavelength; the spectral emission lines seen (Al I, Mg I, Si, Zn, Na, K) that would fall inside 600-1000 nm or 1.3-1.7 um detector bands; beam attenuation by the plume and condensate.
3. Condensate (soot): primary particle and agglomerate sizes, mass generation rate per unit track length or per joule of laser energy for Al alloys, how much reaches windows and cover slides, and the measured cover-slide transmission loss per build hour.
4. Spatter: ejection velocities, angles, size distributions and counts per mm of track for Al alloys versus steels; how far hot spatter travels in argon; how a cross-flow changes this.
5. The time and length scales a monitoring system has to resolve (melt-pool transit time, solidification time, keyhole fluctuation spectrum, spatter speeds) and the frame rates, exposures and bandwidths that published Al LPBF monitoring used.

Give numbers with units and a source for each, flag where Al alloys differ from steels or Ti-6Al-4V, and say where data for Al are missing.
